bib.title: Natural Language Processing with Python, Chapter 5: Categorizing and Tagging Words

question: What are lexical categories, how can words and their categories be stored in Python, and how can each word of a text be tagged automatically with its word class?

results.claim: A default tagger that labels every token NN gets about an eighth of Brown news tokens right.
results.setup: Brown corpus, category news, unsimplified tagset; DefaultTagger('NN') evaluated on the same tagged sentences it was chosen from (no train/test split, nothing is trained).

results.claim: A regular-expression tagger with 8 suffix/number patterns (catch-all NN last) gets about a fifth right.
results.setup: Brown news, unsimplified tags; RegexpTagger with patterns for -ing, -ed, -es, -ould, 's, -s, numbers, default NN; evaluated on all news sentences (no split, nothing trained).
results.note: Prose says 'correct about a fifth of the time'.

results.claim: A lookup tagger storing the most likely tag of only the 100 most frequent words gets nearly half of tokens right (no backoff; unlisted words get None).
results.setup: Brown news, UnigramTagger(model=likely_tags) over the 100 most frequent words, evaluated on all news sentences (same data the table was built from; no backoff in the evaluated version).
results.note: Text then adds NN backoff but prints no accuracy for it; Example 5-4 and Figure 5-4 show accuracy versus model size 2**0..2**14 with NN backoff, values only on the plot, rising fast then plateauing.

results.claim: A unigram tagger trained and tested on the same Brown news sentences scores 93.5%, which overstates real performance.
results.setup: Brown news, UnigramTagger trained on all tagged_sents and evaluated on the same sentences (train = test).

results.claim: With a 90/10 train/test split the unigram tagger drops to 81.2% on held-out sentences.
results.setup: Brown news; first 4160 tagged sentences (90%) train, remaining 10% test; UnigramTagger, no backoff.
results.note: Text prints size = 4160 as the training sentence count; test count is not printed (inferred about 463 from 4160/0.9).
results.where: 5.5 Separating the Training and Testing Data, p.203

results.claim: A bigram tagger with no backoff gets only 10.3% on held-out text because one unseen word yields None for the rest of the sentence.
results.setup: Brown news, same 90/10 split (4160 train sentences); BigramTagger(train_sents), no backoff, evaluated on test_sents.

results.claim: Backing off bigram to unigram to default NN gives 84.5% on held-out text, best result in the chapter.
results.setup: Brown news, 90/10 split; t0 = DefaultTagger('NN'), t1 = UnigramTagger(train, backoff=t0), t2 = BigramTagger(train, backoff=t1); evaluated on test_sents.
results.note: Printed twice with the same value (Combining Taggers p.205 and Example 5-5 p.208).

results.claim: About 1 in 20 trigram contexts (current word plus two previous tags) is ambiguous in the training data, which bounds an n-gram tagger.
results.metric: fraction of trigram tokens in ambiguous contexts
results.setup: All Brown news tagged sentences; context = (tag1, tag2, current word); ambiguous when more than one tag was seen.
results.note: The text says 'a lower bound on the performance of a trigram tagger' but gives no resulting accuracy figure.

results.claim: Tag counts in Brown news (simplified tagset): N is the most frequent tag with 22226 tokens.
results.setup: Brown news, simplified tags, counted with a defaultdict(int); followed by P 10845, DET 10648, NP 8336, V 7313.

results.claim: NN is the most likely tag in Brown news, and a Brill demo on 80 sentences found 6555 candidate useful rules; no Brill accuracy is reported.
results.setup: nltk.tag.brill.demo() on 80 training sentences; rule score = Fixed minus Broken; top rule 'NN -> VB if the tag of the preceding word is TO' scored 12 (fixed 13, broken 1).
results.note: The chapter gives no accuracy for the Brill tagger, only the claim that it performs very well with models a tiny fraction of n-gram size.

results.claim: Brill tagging achieves good performance with models only a tiny fraction of the size of n-gram taggers (asserted, no data).
results.setup: Qualitative statement in 5.6; no size or accuracy numbers given.

limits: Default (0.1309), regexp (0.2033) and lookup (0.4558) accuracies are scored on the same news sentences used to build them, with no held-out split; only the unigram, bigram and backoff numbers use the 90/10 split.
Single split of one Brown category (news); no variance, no cross-validation (exercise 42 leaves split choice to the reader), no other genres or corpora.
No accuracy is reported for the Brill tagger, for trigram backoff, or for the unknown-word UNK approach; they are left to exercises (Your Turn, exercises 30, 32, 36).

Dated APIs (Python 2 and NLTK 2.x): print statements, cPickle, simplify_tags=True, nltk.ibigrams, dict.keys() returning lists and FreqDist.keys() sorted by frequency, nltk.defaultdict, nltk.Index, tagger.evaluate(), nltk.tag.brill.demo(), nltk.pos_tag on word_tokenize output. Current NLTK uses accuracy(), tagset='universal' in place of simplify_tags, FreqDist.most_common(), Python 3 pickle, and the Brill API changed.

Dated method: n-gram, regexp and Brill taggers are 2009-era baselines; the chapter points to Chapter 6 (classifier-based tagging) and Chapter 7 (chunking) and does not cover HMM/CRF or neural taggers.
practices: Start every tagger evaluation from a default baseline that tags everything with the most frequent tag (NN), because it sets the floor (5.4).
Train and test on separate data (90% / 10%); a tagger that memorises its training data scores near perfect and is useless (5.5).
Chain taggers with backoff (bigram, unigram, default) so the specific model handles what it knows and the general one handles the rest (5.5).
Tag at the sentence level; n-gram context must not cross sentence boundaries, and tags before the first word are None (5.5).
Keep n at 3 or lower, since larger n runs into the sparse data problem (5.8).
Replace low-frequency words with UNK so n-gram taggers can use context to tag unseen words (5.3, 5.5).
Use a confusion matrix of gold against predicted tags to find tags to merge or treat specially (5.5).
Save trained taggers to a pickle file instead of retraining (5.5).
Judge a tagset by its use: finer tags give the tagger more left context but more choices per token (5.5, 5.7).
Prefer Brill transformation rules when the model must be small or interpretable (5.6).

terms.definition: The process of classifying words into their parts-of-speech and labeling them accordingly is known as part-of-speech tagging, POS tagging, or simply tagging.
The collection of tags used for a particular task is known as a tagset.
A corpus which has been manually annotated and accepted as a standard against which the guesses of an automatic system are assessed.
For each token, assign the tag that is most likely for that particular token.
A generalization of a unigram tagger whose context is the current word together with the part-of-speech tags of the n-1 preceding tokens.
As n gets larger, the specificity of the contexts increases, as does the chance that the data we wish to tag contains contexts that were not present in the training data.
When a more specialized model (such as a bigram tagger) cannot assign a tag in a given context, we back off to a more general model (such as a unigram tagger).

A kind of transformation-based learning: guess the tag of each word, then go back and fix the mistakes; rules have the form 'replace T1 with T2 in the context C' and are scored by errors corrected minus correct tags broken.
Charts expected tags (the gold standard) against actual tags generated by a tagger.
Nouns are an open class (new members are added); prepositions are a closed class with a limited set that changes only very gradually.
